subject: chemistry
title: Reacting masses from equations
key_idea: A balanced equation shows the ratio in which moles of substances react. Convert the known mass to moles, use the equation ratio to find the moles of the other substance, then convert those moles to a mass.

blocks.text: (Higher tier) The numbers in front of formulae in a balanced equation show the ratio of moles that react.

blocks.label: Reading an equation in moles
where: 1 mole of magnesium reacts with 2 moles of hydrochloric acid.
They produce 1 mole of magnesium chloride and 1 mole of hydrogen gas.

items: The balancing numbers give the mole ratio, not the mass ratio.
In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, the ratio of moles of H₂ to NH₃ is 3 : 2.
Masses of reactants and products can be found from the mass of just one substance.
The balancing numbers in an equation give the ratio of moles.
You need the mass of only one substance to find the mass of another.

sections.heading: Calculating a mass from an equation

blocks.text: Use the same four steps every time. Write the balanced equation first.

items.text: Moles = mass ÷ Mr. Use grams, so convert kilograms or tonnes first.
Multiply by the equation ratio, wanted ÷ known, to find the moles of the other substance.
Mass = moles × Mr of the wanted substance.
Give the unit and the number of significant figures asked for.

blocks.label: Worked example: mass of magnesium oxide from 2.4 g of magnesium
where: The ratio Mg : MgO is 2 : 2, so moles of MgO = 0.10 mol.

diagram.alt: Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide made from a mass of magnesium.
diagram.question: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide made from {m} g of magnesium. (Relative atomic masses: Mg = 24, O = 16)
working: The ratio Mg : MgO is 2 : 2, so moles of MgO = moles of Mg.

items: In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, each 3 moles of H₂ makes 2 moles of NH₃.
Moles of H₂ = moles of NH₃ × 3/2. Moles of NH₃ = moles of H₂ × 2/3.
Check which way round the ratio goes. The wanted substance goes on top.

diagram.alt: Calculate the mass of ammonia made from a mass of hydrogen.
diagram.question: Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Calculate the mass of ammonia made from {m} g of hydrogen. (Relative formula masses: H₂ = 2, NH₃ = 17)
working: Ratio H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2, so moles of NH₃ = moles of H₂ × 2/3

items: Mass to moles, then ratio from the equation, then moles to mass.
The ratio uses the balancing numbers, with the wanted substance on top.
Convert units to grams first. Round as the question asks.

sections.heading: The proportion method and common slips

blocks.text: The same answer can come from masses in proportion. Use the equation to write the mass of each substance in the quantities shown.

blocks.label: Mass in proportion: iron from iron oxide
where: 240 tonnes of Fe₂O₃ gives 240 ÷ 160 × 112 = 168 tonnes of iron.

items: Multiply Mr by the balancing number: 2 × Mr NH₃ = 34 in N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.
Do not forget the balancing numbers. Using 40 × 1.35 = 54 for 2Mg → 2MgO loses marks.
If the question gives masses in tonnes or kilograms, the ratio method still works. Keep the same unit throughout.
Show each step. Marks are given for the Mr, the moles and the final mass.
The proportion method and the moles method give the same answer.
Include the balancing numbers in every step.

checks.q: In the equation Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, how many moles of hydrochloric acid react with 0.5 mol of magnesium?
checks.a: 1.0 mol, because the ratio of Mg to HCl is 1 : 2.

checks.q: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide made when 135 g of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, ferments: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. (Mr: C₆H₁₂O₆ = 180, CO₂ = 44)
Calculate the maximum mass of iron from 240 tonnes of iron oxide, Fe₂O₃. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16)

exam_phrases: allow correct use of an incorrectly calculated value of moles
(from equation 2 moles of Au reacts with 3 moles of Cl₂)

mistakes.right: The ratio is the wrong way round. H₂ : NH₃ is 3 : 2, so moles of H₂ = 1.47 × 3/2 = 2.205.
Chlorine is Cl₂, so the Mr is 71. Mass = 0.00133 × 71.

mistakes.wrong: Answer 0.0946 when the question asks for milligrams.
mistakes.right: The last mark is for the conversion: 0.0946 g = 94.6 mg.

worked_example.question:
Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen to produce ammonia (NH₃). The equation for the reaction is:

N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃

Relative atomic masses (Ar): H = 1, N = 14

Calculate the mass of hydrogen that is needed to produce 25 g of ammonia.
worked_example.tip: Alternative method: 6 g of H₂ gives 34 g of NH₃, so 25 g of NH₃ needs (6 ÷ 34) × 25 = 4.41 g of H₂.

exam_phrases: final answer with or without working scores 3
allow ECF for incorrect formula mass

mistakes.right: The equation makes 2 moles of CO₂ for each mole of glucose. Moles of CO₂ = 0.75 × 2 = 1.5, so the mass is 66 g. The answer 33 scores 2.
This uses Mr as a mass for 1 g. Use 40/24 × 1.35 = 2.25 g, or 80/48 × 1.35 if the equation is written 2Mg → 2MgO.
The equation Fe₂O₃ gives 2 iron atoms, so the iron in 160 tonnes is 112, not 56. The answer 84 scores only 2 marks.

worked_example.question:
Magnesium burns in excess oxygen to form magnesium oxide.

The balanced equation for this reaction is

2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO

Starting with 1.35 g of magnesium, calculate the maximum mass of magnesium oxide that could be formed in this reaction.

(relative atomic masses: O = 16.0, Mg = 24.0)

You must show your working.
answer_points: 1 g of Mg forms 40/24 = 1.67 g of MgO (1)
1.35 g of Mg forms 40/24 × 1.35 = 2.25 g of MgO (1)
worked_example.tip: Moles method: 1.35 ÷ 24 = 0.05625 mol of Mg and so of MgO; 0.05625 × 40 = 2.25 g. Allow follow-through for an incorrect formula mass.

exam_phrases: Mr of H₂S = 34.1 and Mr of SO₂ = 64.1
need both relative formula masses for 1 mark
give your answer to 3 significant figures

mistakes.wrong: Mr of H₂S = 34 and Mr of SO₂ = 64.
mistakes.right: These are not allowed when the Ar values are given as 1.0, 16.0 and 32.1. Use 34.1 and 64.1.

mistakes.wrong: Mr of CaCO₃ = 100 and Mr of CaO = 56.
mistakes.right: 100 and 56 are not allowed. Use the Ar values given: 100.1 and 56.1.

mistakes.wrong: Mass of SO₂ = 3 × 64.1 using the moles of H₂S without checking the ratio.
mistakes.right: Check the ratio first. Here 2H₂S gives 2SO₂, so the ratio is 1 : 1 and the moles are the same.

worked_example.question:
Hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, reacts with oxygen, O₂, to form sulfur dioxide, SO₂, and water.

The balanced symbol equation is shown.

2H₂S(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2SO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)

Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide made from 102.3 g of hydrogen sulfide.

(The relative atomic mass, Ar, of H is 1.0, of O is 16.0 and of S is 32.1.)
answer_points: Mr of H₂S = 34.1 and Mr of SO₂ = 64.1 (1)
worked_example.tip: 192.3 g on the answer line scores all 3 marks. Follow-through is allowed from an incorrect Mr or number of moles.
